word:lxx:L700004.explanation: Aara is a proper name, identifying a person rather than expressing an action, quality, or general idea. In the Greek Septuagint corpus, it occurs once, at 1 Chronicles 8:1. The available lexical information preserves Aara as the name itself and does not provide an additional ordinary-language definition or explanation of its meaning. Therefore, it is best understood simply as a personal name whose precise identity and significance depend on the surrounding genealogical context, which is not included here.

word:lxx:L700141.explanation: Angi, also written Anggi, is a proper name identifying a person in the Greek Old Testament. It is not a general word describing an action, quality, or object. This name occurs twice within one verse in the Greek LXX, Numbers 26:24. Its precise significance there comes from the surrounding passage, but its ordinary function is simply to identify the named individual.

word:lxx:L700318.explanation: Aetos means eagle, the bird named in Scripture.

word:lxx:L700387.explanation: This Greek LXX verb means being “despondent”—deeply discouraged, disheartened, or cast down. As a verb, it describes a person entering or remaining in a state of low courage rather than naming a permanent identity. It occurs eight times in the Greek LXX corpus, chiefly in Old Testament books, with one occurrence in 1 Maccabees. Its precise force in any particular verse depends on the surrounding passage, but its central idea is loss of heart and discouragement.

word:lxx:L700556.explanation: This adjective means “unswerving”: staying firm and not turning aside. It describes someone or something characterized by steady direction, commitment, or purpose rather than hesitation or deviation. The word appears twice in the Greek LXX corpus, both times in 4 Maccabees. Its basic sense is clear from the lexical definition, while the surrounding verse determines precisely what person, action, or quality is being described in each occurrence.

word:lxx:L700611.explanation: Akrotomos means sharp; it describes sharp stone and rock.

word:lxx:L700732.explanation: This Greek LXX adjective means “salty,” describing something that has the taste or character of salt. It is a straightforward word for saltiness rather than a separate title, name, or abstract quality. In the Greek Old Testament, it occurs eight times, in descriptions connected with places and waters. Its exact force in any particular verse depends on the noun it describes and the surrounding passage, but its basic meaning remains the same: having salt or being salt-like in taste.

word:lxx:L700747.explanation: Amada is a personal name, also rendered “Amatha.” It identifies a named individual rather than expressing an action, quality, or general idea. In the Greek Old Testament, this name occurs once, in Genesis 36:26. Because the available text does not include the surrounding verse, its specific role in that genealogy cannot be described here; its lexical function is simply that of a proper name identifying a person.

word:lxx:L700813.explanation: Amessia is a proper name identifying a person named in the Greek Old Testament. It does not describe an action, quality, or general idea; its function is to distinguish one individual from others. The name appears once in the Greek Old Testament, at 1 Chronicles 6:30. Without the surrounding verse text, the person’s specific role or significance cannot be explained from the name alone. The clearest meaning is therefore the personal name “Amessia.”

word:lxx:L700938.explanation: This verb means to accept in turn—to receive or take something when one’s turn comes. It describes an action of accepting rather than a person, object, or quality. In the Greek LXX corpus represented here, it occurs twice, both times in 2 Maccabees. Its precise force in either passage depends on the surrounding verse and sentence, but the central idea remains receiving something successively or in an ordered sequence.

word:lxx:L701029.explanation: This Greek LXX verb means to pierce through or to fix something on a spit. It describes a direct physical action involving piercing and securing an object. The word occurs once in the Greek LXX corpus, in 2 Maccabees 12:22. Without the verse text and its surrounding context, the precise object and situation cannot be stated, but the word’s basic sense remains the act of piercing through or fastening on a spit.

word:lxx:L701076.explanation: This noun means an “outpouring”—something poured out or released in abundance. It describes the result or act of flowing forth, rather than a person or object with a specific identity. In the Greek Old Testament, it occurs twice: once in Habakkuk and once in 3 Maccabees. Its exact force in either passage depends on the surrounding verse and subject, but the central idea remains something issued or poured outward. [p03:word:lxx:L701076:identity] [p03:word:lxx:L701076:occurrences]

word:lxx:L701155.explanation: This Greek LXX verb means “acknowledge in turn.” It describes responding to another acknowledgment with a corresponding recognition. Its basic sense is reciprocal: one person answers by acknowledging what another person has acknowledged. The word occurs six times in the Greek LXX corpus, across Ezra, Psalms, Daniel, Sirach, and 3 Maccabees. Its precise force in any verse depends on the surrounding wording.

word:lxx:L701270.explanation: This adjective describes people, objects, or positions set face to face—that is, directly opposite one another. It expresses a direct arrangement or encounter rather than something distant or merely related. In the Greek Old Testament, it occurs six times across six verses, including passages in Genesis, Exodus, Samuel, Chronicles, and Ezekiel. Its precise force in any particular verse depends on what is being positioned or compared, but its central idea remains direct opposition or correspondence: one side stands directly before the other.

word:lxx:L701353.explanation: This adjective describes something free from interference and therefore uninterrupted. It points to activity, progress, or conditions that continue without obstruction or disruption. In the Greek LXX corpus, it occurs once, in 3 Maccabees 6:28. The word itself gives a general description rather than naming a person or object; the surrounding verse determines what is uninterrupted in that particular setting.

word:lxx:L701564.explanation: This noun means “effluence” or “emanation”: something flowing or proceeding outward from a source. It describes an outflow rather than the source itself, and it can refer to what comes forth from something in a continuous or expressive way. In the Greek LXX corpus, it occurs once, in Wisdom 7:25. Its precise force in that passage depends on the surrounding verse and passage context.

word:lxx:L701586.explanation: Apostasia means distancing or departure. It can describe forsaking someone.

word:lxx:L701605.explanation: This verb means “slung” or “cast.” It describes an action in which something is sent outward rather than simply held or carried. As a verb, it focuses on the act of casting, while the surrounding passage determines what was cast and why. In the Greek LXX corpus represented here, it occurs once, in 4 Maccabees 16:21. That single occurrence identifies it as an action word expressing the movement of something being cast or slung, without by itself specifying the object or purpose.

word:lxx:L701748.explanation: This noun means “excellence” or “prowess”—outstanding ability, strength, or achievement. It describes the quality of someone who performs remarkably well or displays notable power. In the Greek LXX corpus represented here, it occurs once, in 4 Maccabees 12:16, so its precise force in that sentence depends on the surrounding verse and passage. The word’s central idea remains recognized distinction through exceptional ability or strength.

word:lxx:L701850.explanation: This word means “chief cup-bearer,” a noun identifying the leading person connected with serving the ruler’s cup. It refers to an official position rather than to a general description of drinking or hospitality. In the Greek Old Testament, the word occurs eight times, all in Genesis, especially in the account involving Pharaoh’s servants. Its exact significance in any particular verse depends on the surrounding passage, but its basic meaning remains the chief cup-bearer or principal official in that role.

word:lxx:L701977.explanation: “Asobaesd; Asovaezth” is a proper name, functioning as a personal designation rather than a word describing an action, quality, or object. Its precise identity must be taken from the surrounding genealogical passage, since the name itself does not provide an ordinary descriptive meaning. In the Greek LXX corpus, it occurs once, at 1 Chronicles 3:20. The two forms are presented as renderings of the same named entity, not as separate meanings.

word:lxx:L702060.explanation: Asōthi, also rendered Asothi, is a proper name rather than a word describing an action, quality, or object. It identifies a particular person or place in the Greek Old Testament text, though the available information does not specify which. This name occurs once in the Greek LXX corpus, at 1 Chronicles 11:29. Its meaning is therefore its identifying name, not a general concept or instruction.

word:lxx:L702392.explanation: Baithanam, also rendered Vethanam, is a place name listed among cities.

word:lxx:L702536.explanation: Baria, also rendered Varia, is a proper name rather than a word describing an action, quality, or object. It identifies a person in the Greek Old Testament, appearing three times in two verses: twice in Genesis 46:17 and once in Numbers 26:28. The name itself does not provide a general concept or spiritual principle; its meaning is its role as a personal designation. The surrounding verse is needed to identify the individual being named in each occurrence.

word:lxx:L702569.explanation: Basanitis is a proper name for the region of Basan.

word:lxx:L702622.explanation: Beelmōn, also rendered Veelmon, is a proper name rather than a word describing an action, quality, or object. It identifies a named entity in the Greek Old Testament tradition. This name occurs once in the LXX, in Joshua 13:17. Without the verse text, its precise referent cannot be described further here, but the supplied meaning consistently presents it as a name, not a general vocabulary term.

word:lxx:L702657.explanation: Berzelli is a proper name used to identify a person in the Greek Old Testament. It is rendered “Berzelli,” with “Verzelli” also given as a gloss, so it functions as a personal name rather than a word describing an idea, action, or quality. The name occurs ten times across nine verses, from 2 Samuel through Nehemiah. Its precise reference depends on the passage.

word:lxx:L702785.explanation: Boukias, also rendered Vukias, is a personal name rather than a word describing an action, quality, or object. In the Greek Old Testament, it appears twice, both times in 1 Chronicles, at 1 Chronicles 25:4 and 25:13. The available information identifies the name itself but does not provide enough surrounding verse text to explain anything further about the person or his role. Its precise significance in either reference therefore depends on the surrounding passage.

word:lxx:L702819.explanation: This Greek LXX noun means “shower” or “rain,” referring to water falling from the sky. It names ordinary rainfall rather than an action or a person. In the Greek Old Testament, it occurs twice, both times in Psalms, and is rendered “rain” in each occurrence. The word’s basic meaning is therefore clear and concrete: a shower of rain or rainfall. Its precise significance in either psalm depends on the surrounding verse and passage, which are needed to explain how the image functions there.

word:lxx:L702846.explanation: Gaar is a proper name, rendered as “Gaar.” It functions as a name rather than as a common word describing an action, quality, or object. The word occurs once in the Greek LXX, at Nehemiah 7:49, so there is no wider usage pattern available for comparison. Its precise referent must be determined from the surrounding passage, since the name itself does not provide that context.

word:lxx:L702903.explanation: This word means “land” or “country,” referring to a stretch of earth or a particular territory. It is a noun used in the Greek Old Testament and may describe a broad region or the land associated with a people. The word occurs seven times in seven Old Testament verses, including passages in 2 Kings, Ezra, Psalms, and Ezekiel. Its exact sense in any verse depends on whether the surrounding passage emphasizes the territory itself or the people connected with it.

word:lxx:L703045.explanation: This word means “mother,” referring to a female parent. It is a noun used to identify the woman who gives birth to or raises a child. In the Greek LXX, it occurs once, in Wisdom 7:12, and its rendering there is “mother.” The word’s basic meaning is therefore direct and familiar: it names a child’s mother. The particular emphasis or relationship intended in that verse must be understood from the surrounding passage, but the word itself carries this clear family meaning.

word:lxx:L703117.explanation: This adjective means “carved,” describing something shaped by cutting or engraving. It is used in the Greek Old Testament and related writings for objects or images made by human workmanship, especially when distinguishing them from what is naturally occurring or divinely given. The word appears 52 times in this corpus, from Exodus through 1 Maccabees. Its precise force in a particular verse depends on the noun it describes and the surrounding passage.

word:lxx:L703162.explanation: Gomer is a proper name used for a person in the Greek Old Testament. It does not describe an action, quality, or general idea; it identifies someone named Gomer. The name appears twice in this Greek Old Testament corpus, once in Ezekiel 38:6 and once in Hosea 1:3. Without the surrounding verse text, the name itself supports identification but does not establish additional meaning or significance.

word:lxx:L703188.explanation: This noun means “instructor” or “schoolmaster.” It refers to a person who teaches or guides others in learning. In the Greek Old Testament, it appears four times, all in Deuteronomy, so its recorded use is limited to that book’s contexts. The word describes a teaching role rather than an action or quality. Its precise emphasis in any one verse depends on the surrounding passage, which is not included here.

word:lxx:L703221.explanation: Golan is a proper name rendered as “Golan.” In the Greek Old Testament, this word appears once, at 1 Chronicles 6:56. Because the available wording identifies the name but does not include the verse text or surrounding passage, it is best understood here simply as the name Golan rather than assigned an additional meaning or significance. Its precise role in that verse depends on the surrounding context.

word:lxx:L703283.explanation: This is a proper name referring to Daniel, also rendered Thanil. It functions as a personal name rather than a general word describing an object, action, or quality. In the Greek Old Testament and related Greek writings represented here, it occurs 127 times, most often in Daniel and also in Bel and the Dragon, Susanna, 1 Chronicles, Ezekiel, and 4 Maccabees. The name appears across both Old Testament and deuterocanonical books in this LXX corpus.

word:lxx:L703324.explanation: This adjective describes someone who is timid or intimidated—held back by fear, lack of confidence, or a sense of being overawed. In the Greek Old Testament and related Greek Jewish writings represented here, it is used 23 times, so its basic idea recurs across different situations rather than naming one particular emotion or event. The surrounding verse determines whether the person is fearful, lacking courage, or made afraid by another person or circumstance. It describes a condition or attitude, not an action.

word:lxx:L703399.explanation: Delanath is a proper name, rendered “Dēlanath” or “Thilanath.” It identifies a named place or location rather than describing an action, quality, or object in general. In the Greek Old Testament, this name occurs once, at Joshua 17:7. The available lexical information preserves the name itself but does not provide an additional meaning or explanation of its name. Its precise significance in that passage depends on the surrounding verse and its geographical context.

word:lxx:L703474.explanation: This word is a verb that expresses an action or state. Its basic sense is “steal at different times”. It describes stealing that happens on separate occasions, rather than referring only to one isolated act. In the Greek Old Testament, it occurs twice, with both occurrences in 2 Samuel 19:4. The surrounding verse determines how this action is expressed there. Its meaning remains focused on repeated or distinct acts of stealing, not on a broader idea.

word:lxx:L703540.explanation: This verb means to “attempt” or “test”—to try something or put it to the test. It describes an action rather than a person, object, or quality. In the Greek LXX corpus represented here, it occurs once, in 3 Maccabees 5:40. The surrounding verse is needed to determine whether the action emphasizes making an attempt, examining something, or testing someone in that particular setting.

word:lxx:L703643.explanation: This verb means to whisper among themselves, describing quiet speech shared privately by a group. It focuses on speaking softly to one another rather than addressing people openly. In the Greek LXX corpus represented here, it occurs once, in Sirach 12:18. The wording identifies an action, while the surrounding verse would be needed to determine the exact situation or force of that whispering. Its central idea remains discreet, low-voiced conversation among people.

word:lxx:L703706.explanation: This adjective means “bipartite” or “in two parts.” It describes something divided into, or consisting of, two distinct sections. In the Greek LXX, it occurs once, in Daniel 2:41. The word itself identifies a two-part structure, while the surrounding verse determines what divided or combined thing is being described. It is a descriptive term rather than a name for a person, place, or action.

word:lxx:L703759.explanation: This noun means “faction”: a divided group formed when people separate from one another rather than act as one. It describes the condition or presence of such division, not a person’s name or an action by itself. In the Greek LXX corpus, it occurs once, in 1 Maccabees 3:29. Its precise force in that passage depends on the surrounding verse and passage context.

word:lxx:L703801.explanation: Dorkas means a kind of deer.

word:lxx:L703980.explanation: This adjective describes something hollow or something that sinks into hollows. It presents a physical shape or condition rather than an action, person, or abstract quality. In the Greek Old Testament, it occurs twice, both times in Leviticus 13, at Leviticus 13:30 and 13:31. Its precise force in either verse depends on the surrounding passage, but its central sense remains a hollowed or inward-sinking appearance.

word:lxx:L704044.explanation: Ezekias is a proper name—the Greek Old Testament form of a person’s name, not a word describing an action or quality. It identifies King Ezekias, who appears repeatedly in the historical books and in Isaiah, with two further occurrences in Sirach. The name occurs 97 times in the Greek LXX corpus, so its function remains consistent: it points to this individual whenever it appears. Its precise significance in any particular verse comes from the surrounding passage, but the name itself functions as a personal designation.

word:lxx:L704123.explanation: This Greek LXX verb means “sail into” or “enter.” It describes movement into a place, with the wording especially suited to arriving by ship or boat. In this corpus it occurs twice, once in 2 Maccabees and once in 4 Maccabees. The surrounding verse text would determine whether the emphasis falls on the voyage itself or simply on entering. It is a practical action word describing arrival or passage into a destination.

word:lxx:L704181.explanation: Ekei means there, pointing to a place already mentioned.

word:lxx:L704202.explanation: This Greek Old Testament verb means to “purge” or “clear away”—to remove something unwanted so that it is gone. It can describe clearing land, removing people from among a community, or cleansing away impurity, but its central idea remains decisive removal. In the Greek Old Testament, it occurs five times, in Deuteronomy, Joshua, Judges, and Isaiah. Its precise force in any verse depends on what is being removed and the surrounding passage.

word:lxx:L704277.explanation: This Greek LXX verb means “spread out.” It describes the action of extending something outward rather than keeping it gathered or confined. The word appears ten times in the Greek Old Testament and deuterocanonical corpus, showing a recurring action that can be understood from its immediate sentence and surrounding context. Its basic sense remains focused on outward extension or dispersal, while the precise object being spread depends on the verse in which it occurs.

word:lxx:L704350.explanation: Ektypōma means a figure in relief.

word:lxx:L704431.explanation: This word expresses the necessity of coming: “one must come.” It functions as an adjective describing something required or destined to happen, rather than simply reporting that someone comes. It occurs once in the Greek LXX corpus, in 2 Maccabees 6:17. Its precise force in that passage depends on the surrounding verse and passage, but its central meaning is the requirement that someone come.

word:lxx:L704527.explanation: This noun refers to low, wet ground beside rivers—a marsh or meadow shaped by nearby water. It describes a physical landscape rather than an action or quality. In the Greek Old Testament and related Greek writings represented here, it occurs 12 times, including passages associated with the Nile, rivers, and land affected by dryness. The central idea remains land that is low and naturally connected with water. Its precise reference in any particular verse depends on the surrounding passage.

word:lxx:L704552.explanation: This word means “putting into,” describing the act of placing something inside or introducing it. It is a noun, so it names that action rather than expressing a command to perform it. In the Greek LXX corpus, it occurs once, in 3 Maccabees 4:7. The precise significance of the action in that passage depends on the surrounding verse and passage, but the word’s basic sense remains the act of putting something into something else.

word:lxx:L704628.explanation: Emphanizō means to make something apparent or visible.

word:lxx:L704725.explanation: This noun refers to a pledge—something taken or given as security for an obligation. It can describe the act of taking property as a pledge or the pledged item itself. In the Greek Old Testament, it occurs three times, all in Ezekiel 18, where it is rendered “pledge.” Its central idea is a possession connected with a debt or promise, held as security until the obligation is fulfilled. The precise force in each occurrence depends on its surrounding verse and passage.

word:lxx:L704790.explanation: Enteinō means to bend, as when a bow is bent.

word:lxx:L704853.explanation: This noun means “blotting out” or “destruction”—the removal or wiping away of something until it is gone. In the Greek Old Testament, it appears twice, in Ezekiel and Micah, and describes a decisive end rather than a temporary difficulty. As a noun, it names the act or result of being erased, removed, or destroyed. The surrounding verse determines whether the emphasis falls on the act of wiping out or on the destruction that follows.

word:lxx:L704970.explanation: This noun refers to scorn or contempt—the attitude of treating someone or something as beneath respect or worth. It names disdain rather than an action or a person. In the Greek Old Testament, it occurs once, at Psalm 89:5, so its precise force there depends on the surrounding verse and passage. Its central meaning remains the idea of contempt: a low estimation that dismisses or dishonors its object.

word:lxx:L705069.explanation: This verb means to “interrogate; inquire of”—to ask someone for information or seek an answer. It can describe ordinary questioning as well as a serious request for guidance, depending on the surrounding passage. In the Greek Old Testament and related deuterocanonical writings, it occurs 61 times, showing a repeated action of asking, questioning, or seeking an answer rather than a single specialized act. Its precise force in any particular verse depends on who is asking, whom they address, and what information or guidance they seek.

word:lxx:L705115.explanation: This adjective describes someone or something as “skillful” or “clever.” It points to ability, competence, or practical intelligence rather than merely identifying a person or object. In the Greek Old Testament, it occurs once, at Ezra 5:8. Because the verse text and surrounding context are not included here, the word’s precise force in that passage cannot be stated beyond this central meaning. Its basic sense remains a positive description of capable, intelligent action or character.

word:lxx:L705230.explanation: This adverb means “on the surface” or “superficially.” It describes something done or understood only at an outward or shallow level, rather than with depth. In ordinary reading, it can point to an appearance, judgment, or action that does not reach beneath what is immediately visible. The word occurs once in the Greek LXX corpus, in 3 Maccabees 2:31. Its precise force in that verse depends on the surrounding wording, but its basic sense remains a contrast between surface-level treatment and deeper understanding.

word:lxx:L705285.explanation: This verb means “collect together”: to bring people or things together into one gathering. It describes an action of gathering rather than a person, object, or quality. In the Greek Old Testament, it occurs once, in Numbers 17:7. The word’s basic sense is therefore focused and specific: things or people are assembled together, while the surrounding verse determines exactly what is being gathered and for what immediate purpose.

word:lxx:L705322.explanation: This verb means to impose something on someone or to inflict something upon them. It describes an action brought forcefully or deliberately against a person or situation. In the Greek Old Testament and related Greek writings represented here, it occurs 16 times, including passages from Genesis, 1 Samuel, and other books. The surrounding context determines whether the imposed or inflicted thing is a burden, harm, judgment, or another action; the core idea remains placing something upon someone or causing it to be experienced.

word:lxx:L705414.explanation: In the Greek Old Testament, this word is identified as “Ereō; Ereo” and functions as a proper name. Its precise reference or role must be understood from the sentence where it appears, since no verse text is available here. It occurs 3,328 times in the Greek LXX corpus, from Genesis through Song of Songs, so it is broadly distributed rather than limited to one passage or book.

word:lxx:L705560.explanation: This verb means to ennoble someone or to treat and honor them nobly. It describes an action that gives dignity or expresses honorable conduct toward another person, rather than merely identifying a person’s status. In the Greek Old Testament corpus represented here, it occurs once, in 2 Maccabees 10:13. The surrounding verse would be needed to explain exactly how this honorable treatment functions in that passage.

word:lxx:L705678.explanation: Eurythmos means rhythmical, with a harmonious quality.

word:lxx:L705692.explanation: Eustatheia means stability, a firm and well-established condition.

word:lxx:L705771.explanation: This adjective describes someone or something marked by wanton behavior or insolence—boldly disrespectful, offensive, or lacking proper restraint. It presents a quality rather than an action, so the surrounding sentence determines exactly whom or what it describes. In the Greek LXX, it occurs once, in Wisdom 17:7. Its stated meaning is “wanton; insolent,” and no broader sense is established here.

word:lxx:L705872.explanation: This Greek LXX noun means “jealousy” or “rivalry”—the troubled concern that another person may possess, receive, or claim what one regards as belonging to oneself. It names an attitude or condition rather than an action. In the Greek Old Testament, it occurs four times, all in Numbers 5, where the term belongs to the law concerning a husband’s jealousy. Its precise force in any individual verse depends on the surrounding passage, but its central sense is jealousy expressed as suspicion or rivalry.

word:lxx:L705898.explanation: This word means “leavened,” describing something prepared with leaven rather than left unleavened. It refers to a food made to rise or become fermented through the presence of leaven. In the Greek Old Testament, it appears once, in Leviticus 7:13, so its ordinary meaning is clear even though its precise role in that passage depends on the surrounding verse and offering instructions.

word:lxx:L705951.explanation: The word means “Hēth,” functioning as a noun or name rather than describing an action or quality. In this Greek Old Testament corpus, it occurs once, at Psalms 118:57. Because the verse text and broader context are unavailable here, its precise role in that occurrence cannot be explained further. It should therefore be understood simply as the name Hēth, without adding another English meaning.

word:lxx:L706051.explanation: This Greek LXX noun means “watercourse,” referring to a channel or stream through which water flows. It appears three times in the Greek Old Testament, all in 1 Kings 18, where the word identifies a physical feature associated with the altar and its surrounding trench. Its basic sense is therefore geographical and concrete: a place or passage carrying water, rather than water considered simply as a substance. The precise force in any individual verse depends on the surrounding passage.

word:lxx:L706107.explanation: Tharaka is a proper name, referring to a specific named figure rather than describing a general quality, action, or object. In the Greek Old Testament, this name appears twice, once in 2 Kings 19:9 and once in Isaiah 37:9. Those references are parallel accounts, but the available information here does not provide the surrounding verse text or additional details about the person named. The word itself functions as a personal designation: it identifies someone by name.

word:lxx:L706172.explanation: This noun means “determination”: a firm intention or settled will to do something. It describes purposeful resolve rather than a passing thought or wish. In the Greek Old Testament and related deuterocanonical books, it appears 13 times, showing that it can describe determined purpose in different settings. Its precise force in a particular passage depends on the surrounding sentence, but its central idea remains a deliberate decision or strong resolve. The word occurs in both Old Testament and deuterocanonical portions of the LXX corpus.

word:lxx:L706198.explanation: This word refers to a maid or handmaid—a female servant in a household. As a noun, it identifies the woman serving in that role rather than describing an action. In the Greek Old Testament, it occurs four times, all within four Old Testament verses. Its use includes household servants mentioned in Exodus and a handmaid considered in Job, so the central idea is a woman under another household’s authority or service. The exact force in any one verse depends on the surrounding passage.

word:lxx:L706275.explanation: This noun means “oppression” or “affliction”: suffering imposed on people or endured as a heavy burden. In the Greek Old Testament, it describes distress serious enough to be recognized and brought before God, but its precise force in either passage depends on the surrounding verse and context. The word occurs twice in the Greek Old Testament, once in Exodus 3:9 and once in Deuteronomy 26:7. In both recorded renderings, it is translated “affliction,” reinforcing the sense of painful hardship rather than a minor inconvenience.

word:lxx:L706316.explanation: This word means “noise; bustle,” referring to a noisy disturbance or busy commotion. As a noun, it names the sound or activity itself rather than describing an action. In the Greek Old Testament corpus, it occurs twice, in Wisdom 1:10 and 1 Maccabees 9:39. One recorded rendering is “noise,” which fits the central sense. The surrounding verse text is needed to determine whether the word emphasizes loud sound, public commotion, or general disturbance in either passage.

word:lxx:L706349.explanation: Thyō means to sacrifice or immolate.

word:lxx:L706419.explanation: This word is a proper name: “Ianoue” or “Ianue.” It identifies a person by name rather than describing an action, quality, or object. In the Greek Old Testament (LXX), it occurs once, at 1 Chronicles 3:7. The surrounding verse text is not available here, so the name itself does not establish the person’s role, family connection, or significance in that passage.

word:lxx:L706446.explanation: Iasol is a personal name, referring to an individual rather than expressing an action, quality, or general idea. In the Greek Old Testament, it occurs once, in Zechariah 14:5. The available information identifies the name itself but does not provide enough surrounding verse text to explain who Iasol is or what role the person has in that passage. Its precise significance there must therefore be understood from the surrounding context of Zechariah 14:5.

word:lxx:L706503.explanation: Idoumaia is a proper name used for a place.

word:lxx:L706608.explanation: This adjective means “priestly” or “for the priest's office.” It describes something connected with the role or service of a priest, marking it as belonging to priestly use or responsibility rather than describing an ordinary object or activity. word:lxx:L706697.explanation: This word is a proper name identifying a person, rather than a term describing an action, quality, or object. The name’s precise role in that genealogy depends on the surrounding verse text, which is not included here; its basic meaning is simply a personal designation.

word:lxx:L706789.explanation: This noun means “chariot-road,” referring to a road or course intended for chariots. It names a route associated with the movement or racing of chariots rather than a person, action, or abstract idea. In the Greek Old Testament and related Greek writings represented here, it occurs five times, in Genesis and 3 Maccabees. Its exact sense in any particular verse depends on how the surrounding passage uses the road, but its central meaning remains a roadway or course for chariots.

word:lxx:L706815.explanation: Iseriēl, also rendered Iseril, is a proper name referring to a particular person rather than expressing an action, quality, or general idea. In the Greek Old Testament, it occurs once, in 1 Chronicles 25:14. The name itself identifies the individual, but without the verse text and surrounding passage, its specific family connection or role cannot be stated responsibly. Its meaning should therefore be understood as a personal designation within that genealogical or historical record.

word:lxx:L707063.explanation: This noun means “evil-doing”: the carrying out of actions that are morally wrong or harmful. It names wrongdoing as an activity rather than describing a person who does it. In the Greek Old Testament and related Greek writings represented in this corpus, it occurs twice—once in Ezra and once in 3 Maccabees. The word’s basic sense remains focused on the practice or act of doing evil; the surrounding passage determines what particular wrongdoing is meant in each occurrence.

word:lxx:L707166.explanation: This LXX Greek verb means “enjoy the fruits of”: it describes receiving or benefiting from the results or produce connected with something. It is an action word, so it focuses on what someone does with an outcome rather than merely naming the fruit itself. In the Greek Old Testament represented here, it occurs twice, in Joshua 5:12 and Proverbs 8:19. The surrounding verse determines whether the phrase points to literal produce or a broader result.

word:lxx:L707210.explanation: This Greek LXX verb means to bring someone’s life to an end—that is, to cause a person to die. It describes an action rather than a person, object, or abstract quality. The word occurs once in the Greek Old Testament tradition represented here, in Amos 7:12. Its precise force in that verse depends on the surrounding wording, but its central meaning remains clear: ending a person’s life. This is a distinct LXX word and should not be treated as a Greek New Testament lexical entry.

word:lxx:L707337.explanation: Katanath is a proper name that identifies a named person, place, or other entity rather than describing an action or quality. Its meaning is preserved as the name “Katanath,” so no broader definition is supplied. In the Greek Old Testament, it occurs once, at Joshua 19:15. The surrounding verse would be needed to identify exactly what Katanath names there; the word itself functions as a designation, not as a descriptive term.

word:lxx:L707342.explanation: This noun means “observation” or a “means of observing”—the act or method of paying attention in order to notice or understand something. It describes observation itself rather than a person who observes or the thing being observed. In the Greek Old Testament, it occurs once, in Sirach 41:23. Its precise force in that passage depends on the surrounding verse and context, but its central idea remains careful attention or the process by which something is examined and understood.

word:lxx:L707401.explanation: This Greek LXX verb means to cover something with silver. It describes the action of applying silver as a covering or surface treatment, rather than naming the silver itself. The word occurs once in the Greek Old Testament, at Exodus 27:17. Its precise role in that verse depends on the surrounding passage, but its basic meaning remains the act of silver-covering.

word:lxx:L707535.explanation: This Greek LXX noun means “settlement” or “settling.” It refers to establishing residence in a place or to the settled condition that results. The word is used 25 times in the Greek Old Testament and related LXX writings, so it can describe places where people live as well as the act of making a home or dwelling. Its exact emphasis—whether the process of settling or the resulting settlement—depends on the sentence in which it appears.

word:lxx:L707580.explanation: Keblaam, also rendered Kevlaam, is a proper name in the Greek Old Testament. It functions as a personal or place name rather than as a word describing an action, quality, or object. The name occurs once in the Greek LXX, at 2 Kings 15:10. The available lexical information preserves the name itself but does not explain its etymology or identify more specifically what or whom it names. Its precise reference therefore belongs to the surrounding verse and passage.

word:lxx:L707658.explanation: This noun means “formation of honeycombs”: it names the process by which honeycomb structures come into being, rather than a person, creature, or finished object. It occurs once in the Greek LXX corpus, in 4 Maccabees 14:19. Because the surrounding verse text is not included here, the word’s particular force in that sentence cannot be described further; its lexical meaning remains focused on the forming of honeycombs. The term is therefore a precise noun for honeycomb formation.

word:lxx:L707733.explanation: This word means “oven,” referring to a heated place used for baking or cooking. In the Greek Old Testament, it is used twelve times, including descriptions of ovens connected with food preparation and with the effects of intense heat. Its basic sense remains practical and concrete: a structure or appliance in which food is baked. The surrounding passage determines what is being baked or how the oven is being mentioned.

word:lxx:L707791.explanation: Kollaō means to cling closely. It can also mean to join oneself to others, as Ruth was told to join herself to the damsels.

word:lxx:L707874.explanation: This noun means “power” or “might”—the strength or capacity to accomplish something. It describes effective force rather than merely an inward feeling or intention. Its normal sense points to strength that enables action or achievement.

word:lxx:L707896.explanation: Krēnē means a well. It can also mean a spring.

word:lxx:L708048.explanation: Labōemath, also rendered Lavoemath, is a proper name in the Greek Old Testament. word:lxx:L708105.explanation: Latousiim is a proper name, also given as Latusim. It identifies a particular person rather than expressing an action, quality, or general idea. word:lxx:L708264.explanation: Lydia; Lithia is a proper name, referring to a person or place identified by that name. word:lxx:L708286.explanation: Lychnia means a lamp stand used for light.

word:lxx:L708361.explanation: Maeber (also known as Maever) is a proper name in the Greek Old Testament. It identifies a person or place rather than expressing an action, quality, or general idea. Because no verse text or surrounding context is available here, its precise referent must be determined from that passage rather than from the name alone.

word:lxx:L708453.explanation: “Malchia; Malkhia” is a proper name identifying a person, rather than a word describing an action, quality, or object. Those details would require the surrounding verse and passage, which are not included here.

word:lxx:L708570.explanation: Maspha, also written Masfa, is a proper name used for a place in the Greek Old Testament. It identifies that named location rather than describing an action, quality, or relationship. The name occurs twice in the Greek Old Testament, once in Joshua and once in 2 Chronicles. Because the word is a place-name, its precise significance in either passage comes from the surrounding verse and geographic context, not from a general abstract meaning.

word:lxx:L708729.explanation: This noun refers to “blame” or “censure”—an expression of finding fault or reproach. It names the criticism directed toward someone rather than an action of forgiving, helping, or judging. In the Greek LXX corpus, it occurs four times: three times in Job and once in Wisdom. Its precise force in any particular passage depends on the surrounding verse and its subject, but its central idea remains an accusation or expression of fault-finding.

word:lxx:L708776.explanation: This Greek LXX verb means “fill” or “full of,” describing something becoming filled or being full. It presents fullness as a condition or developing state rather than naming a specific object by itself. The word occurs twice in the Greek LXX corpus, both times in 3 Maccabees. Its precise force in either passage depends on what is said to be filled and the surrounding sentence, but the central idea remains fullness or being filled.

word:lxx:L708831.explanation: This adjective describes something raised up from the ground or hanging above it. It can refer to a physical position, emphasizing elevation rather than something resting on the earth. In the Greek Old Testament and related deuterocanonical books, it occurs 16 times, so its basic sense is used across several passages and settings. The surrounding verse determines whether the word points to something suspended, lifted, or positioned above the ground. Its core idea remains simple: elevated, suspended, or hanging rather than grounded.

word:lxx:L708893.explanation: This Greek LXX adverb expresses doubt or rejection, meaning “not perhaps; much less.” It can qualify a thought by questioning whether something is possible and then strengthening the denial by saying that an even greater possibility is out of the question. This word occurs once in the Greek LXX, in Daniel 2:11. Its precise force in that verse depends on the surrounding wording and question.

word:lxx:L708927.explanation: Misa is a proper name—the personal name of an individual in the Greek Old Testament. It occurs once in the LXX, at 1 Chronicles 8:9. Since the name itself identifies a person rather than describing an action, quality, or object, its basic meaning is simply the person’s name, Misa. The surrounding verse is needed to explain that individual’s place in the genealogy, but the lexical sense remains a personal name.

word:lxx:L709021.explanation: Mosolamoth is a proper name preserved as “Mosolamōth” or “Mosolamoth” in the Greek Septuagint. It identifies a person rather than expressing a general action, quality, or idea. The name occurs once in the LXX corpus, at 2 Chronicles 28:12. The available lexical information gives the name’s form but does not provide a further meaning or etymological explanation, so it is best understood simply as the individual’s name in that passage.

word:lxx:L709083.explanation: The word means “mystic,” referring to a person described by that designation. It is a noun, so it names someone rather than expressing an action or quality. In the Greek LXX corpus represented here, it appears once, in Wisdom 8:4. Without the verse text and its surrounding passage, no more specific contextual force can be stated; the supported lexical meaning is simply “mystic.”

word:lxx:L709124.explanation: Naarai, also rendered Naare, is a proper name referring to a person rather than describing an action, quality, or object. In the Greek LXX, this name occurs once, at 1 Chronicles 11:37. Because the verse text and surrounding passage are not included here, the name’s personal identity and role must be learned from that passage rather than from the name itself. Its basic meaning is therefore a personal designation: Naarai or Naare.

word:lxx:L709245.explanation: This noun means a “diadem” or a “sign of consecration”—a visible headpiece or mark associated with being set apart. It refers to an outward sign of sacred appointment or dedication, rather than describing an ordinary ornament alone. In the Greek LXX, this word occurs once, at 2 Kings 11:12. Its precise significance in that passage depends on the surrounding verse and scene.

word:lxx:L709317.explanation: Nisia is a proper name, functioning as the personal designation of someone named Nisia. It is not presented here as a general word describing an action, quality, or object. In the Greek Septuagint, this name occurs once, at Nehemiah 7:56. Without the verse text and its surrounding passage, no further identification or contextual detail can be stated from the name alone.

word:lxx:L709362.explanation: This verb means “make a den”—to create or prepare a sheltered place where something can live. It is a Greek LXX verb found once in the Greek Old Testament, at Isaiah 13:22. Because the word appears only once and the verse text is not included here, its precise force in that sentence depends on the surrounding passage. Its basic idea remains straightforward: forming a den or dwelling place rather than merely being present in one.

word:lxx:L709388.explanation: “Slumber” refers to a state of sleep or drowsiness. As a noun, the word names this condition rather than describing sleeping as an action. In the Greek LXX, it occurs once, at Job 33:15. The word presents sleep or drowsiness as a recognizable condition, while the precise force of its use there depends on the surrounding passage. Its basic meaning is simple: slumber, a state of being asleep or very sleepy.

word:lxx:L709443.explanation: This adjective means “eightieth,” describing something that holds the position of number eighty in an ordered sequence. It is an ordinal term, so it identifies rank or place rather than simply expressing the number eighty by itself. In the Greek LXX corpus represented here, it occurs once, in 2 Maccabees 1:9. The surrounding verse is needed to determine exactly what the adjective describes there.

word:lxx:L709559.explanation: Oldan, also rendered Olthan, is a proper name identifying a person in the Greek Old Testament. It appears twice in this Greek Old Testament corpus, once in 2 Kings 22:14 and once in 2 Chronicles 34:22. Because it is a personal name rather than a descriptive word, its basic meaning is the person’s name itself; the surrounding verse is needed to explain that person’s specific role or actions.

word:lxx:L709674.explanation: This verb means “pare nails,” describing the act of trimming or cutting nails. It is an action word rather than a name for the nail itself. In the Greek Old Testament, it occurs eight times, with most occurrences in Leviticus and Deuteronomy and one later occurrence in 2 Samuel. Its precise force in any particular verse depends on the surrounding wording, but its ordinary meaning remains the practical action of paring or trimming nails.

word:lxx:L709696.explanation: This adverb means “backwards,” describing movement or direction toward the rear rather than forward. It occurs once in the Greek Old Testament, in Genesis 9:23. As an adverb, it modifies an action by indicating how or in what direction something is done. Its basic sense is straightforward, while the exact force in that verse depends on the surrounding sentence and passage. The word itself focuses on backward direction, not on a separate moral or spiritual idea.

word:lxx:L709858.explanation: Houtos means “this” and can also refer to “he.” In context, it points to the person or thing being identified, as in “these things” for things already named.

word:lxx:L709991.explanation: This word means “altogether” or “entirely.” As an adverb, it strengthens a statement by expressing completeness or an unrestricted extent. It can describe something as wholly so, rather than partly or only to a limited degree. In the Greek LXX corpus represented here, it occurs four times, all in 2 Maccabees. Its exact force in any particular sentence depends on the surrounding words, but its central idea is totality or complete extent.

word:lxx:L710038.explanation: This Greek LXX verb means “station”: to place or assign someone in a particular position or location. It describes an act of setting a person where they are intended to stand or serve, rather than merely describing the person’s presence. The word occurs once in the Greek LXX corpus, in 2 Maccabees 12:3. Its precise force in that verse depends on the surrounding passage, but its central idea is deliberate placement or appointment in a position.

word:lxx:L710113.explanation: This word is a verb that expresses an action or state. Its basic sense is “by this time”. It points to a time already reached by the moment under discussion, functioning as a time expression rather than naming a person, object, or event. In the Greek Old Testament, it appears once, in Psalms 69:4. Since the verse text and surrounding passage are not included here, the word’s precise force in that sentence must be understood from its context. Its ordinary contribution is to mark something as occurring or being true by that time.

word:lxx:L710254.explanation: Penia means poverty, a condition of need.

word:lxx:L710320.explanation: This verb means “stand around” or “stand clear.” It describes people taking a standing position around something or keeping themselves apart from it, depending on the sentence. In the Greek Old Testament and related deuterocanonical books, it occurs six times, including passages from Joshua, Samuel, and 2 Maccabees. Its basic idea remains physical positioning: being situated around something or deliberately standing away from it. The surrounding words determine which sense is intended in a particular verse.

word:lxx:L710395.explanation: This Greek LXX verb means “turn around”: to change direction by turning from one way toward another. It describes an action or movement rather than a person, object, or abstract quality. The word occurs three times in the Greek Old Testament represented here, appearing once in Genesis and twice in Numbers. Its precise force in any particular verse depends on what or whom the subject turns toward, but its central idea remains a physical or directional turning around.

word:lxx:L710412.explanation: Periphrassō means to fence all around.

word:lxx:L710841.explanation: This Greek LXX verb means “spit forth,” describing the act of forcefully ejecting something from the mouth. word:lxx:L710904.explanation: This Greek LXX noun means “addition” or “increase”—something added or made greater. word:lxx:L711042.explanation: This Greek LXX noun means “vanguard,” referring to those who go at the front or lead the way. word:lxx:L711110.explanation: Pyrseuō means to light up or kindle.

word:lxx:L711363.explanation: This noun means “pack” or “baggage,” referring to the belongings or load that someone carries. It occurs once in the Greek Old Testament corpus, in 2 Maccabees 3:25. word:lxx:L711433.explanation: Sama is a proper name, referring to a person rather than describing an idea, action, or quality. word:lxx:L711491.explanation: This Greek LXX noun means a “board” or “plank,” referring to a flat, solid piece of wood. It is a concrete word for a wooden piece used in construction or other practical purposes, rather than an abstract idea. It occurs three times in the Greek Old Testament, in 2 Kings, Ezekiel, and Song of Songs. Its precise significance in any one passage depends on the surrounding verse and context.

word:lxx:L711558.explanation: Sava is a proper name, identifying a person rather than describing an action, quality, or object. Its lexical meaning is therefore the personal designation “Sava”; any further significance depends on the surrounding passage, not on the name itself.

word:lxx:L711635.explanation: The LXX word Sekelak is a proper name, rather than a common word describing an action, quality, or object. word:lxx:L711680.explanation: This word is a proper name, rendered as “Semmēr” or “Semmir,” rather than a term describing an action, quality, or object. word:lxx:L711806.explanation: Siteomai means to take food or eat.

word:lxx:L711859.explanation: Hard-heartedness describes an inward condition of stubbornness or resistance, especially a heart that is not soft, responsive, or willing to change. word:lxx:L712106.explanation: This Greek LXX verb means “glisten”: to shine or give off a bright, noticeable gleam. The word occurs six times in the Greek LXX corpus represented here, including Old Testament and deuterocanonical writings. It is uncommon but appears across several biblical books. Its precise force in any particular verse depends on the surrounding passage.

word:lxx:L712274.explanation: Symaer (also rendered “Simaer”) is a proper name rather than a word describing an action, quality, or object. This name occurs once in the LXX corpus, at Numbers 26:36, and no wider meaning or thematic use is established by the available information. Its significance in that verse must therefore be understood from the surrounding passage.

word:lxx:L712340.explanation: Sympolemeō means to join in war.

word:lxx:L712421.explanation: This Greek LXX noun means “convergence,” referring to people, things, or movements coming together at one point. It describes a gathering or meeting rather than an individual object or action. The word occurs once in the Greek LXX corpus, in 3 Maccabees 3:8. Its precise force in that passage depends on the surrounding verse and context, but its central idea remains the joining or assembling of separate things into one place or meeting.

word:lxx:L712483.explanation: A noun meaning “knowing along with.” It refers to someone who shares knowledge of a matter with another person—one who knows alongside or together with someone else. In the Greek Old Testament, this word appears once, at Job 16:19. Because the verse text and surrounding context are not included here, its precise role in that passage cannot be described further; its central sense remains shared or accompanying knowledge.

word:lxx:L712524.explanation: This noun means “being reared together” or “common nurture”—the shared upbringing that creates a bond between people who grow up together. It points to a relationship formed through life under the same care, rather than merely describing people who happen to meet. In the Greek Old Testament corpus represented here, it occurs twice, in 3 Maccabees 5:32 and 4 Maccabees 13:22. The surrounding verse text is needed to determine the precise force of the word in either passage.

word:lxx:L712599.explanation: This verb means to complain of hardship, especially by expressing that complaint angrily. It describes spoken protest or grumbling when someone feels burdened or distressed, rather than simply naming a hardship itself. In the Greek Old Testament, it occurs twice, both times in 4 Maccabees. Its precise force in either passage depends on the surrounding sentence, but the central idea remains an aggrieved complaint voiced with strong feeling.

word:lxx:L712717.explanation: Tapeinoō means to humble or bring low.

word:lxx:L712762.explanation: This verb means “bear children”—to give birth or have children. It describes childbearing rather than naming the children themselves. In the Greek Old Testament, it occurs seven times, including passages in Genesis, Isaiah, and Jeremiah. Its precise emphasis may be the act of bearing children or the resulting children, depending on the surrounding sentence. The word therefore points to becoming a parent through childbirth.

word:lxx:L712788.explanation: This verb means to collect taxes—the act of gathering required payments. In the Greek Old Testament corpus represented here, it occurs twice, both within one verse: 1 Maccabees 13:39. The word’s precise force in that verse depends on the surrounding passage, but its basic meaning remains the collection of taxes.

word:lxx:L712810.explanation: This adverb means “in orderly manner,” describing an action carried out in an arranged, orderly way rather than randomly or chaotically. In the Greek LXX corpus, it occurs once, in 1 Maccabees 6:40; the surrounding verse text is needed to explain its particular use there.

word:lxx:L712937.explanation: This LXX adjective means “thirtieth,” describing something that holds the ordinal position of number thirty. word:lxx:L712942.explanation: This word means “of three years” or “three years old.” It describes a person, animal, or thing in relation to an age of three years, and it can function as either a noun or an adjective. Its basic meaning is straightforward; the surrounding verse determines what is three years old or what three-year period is being described.

word:lxx:L713178.explanation: This word means “officiate; serve.” It is a verb describing the act of carrying out service or performing a duty. In this Greek LXX corpus, it occurs five times, all in the deuterocanonical books represented here: four times in Wisdom and once in Sirach. Its central idea is active service—someone functioning in a serving role rather than merely being identified as a servant. Its precise force in any one passage depends on the surrounding sentence.

word:lxx:L713192.explanation: Hypodeiknymi means to show or indicate something.

word:lxx:L713260.explanation: This adjective describes someone who owes a debt or is under an obligation to repay what is owed. In the Greek Old Testament, it occurs twice, once in 1 Samuel 22:2 and once in Isaiah 50:1. Its precise force in either passage depends on the surrounding verse and context.

word:lxx:L713422.explanation: This word is a proper name rendered “Pherezaios” or “Ferezeos,” identifying a people mentioned in the Greek Old Testament. It is not a general description or action word, but the designation of this particular people. The word occurs 21 times in the Greek Old Testament, from Genesis through Nehemiah, with references especially in Exodus and Joshua. Its precise significance in any individual verse depends on the surrounding passage.

word:lxx:L713457.explanation: This adjective describes someone or something as “fond of good”—drawn toward what is good and valuing it. It expresses a positive affection for goodness rather than merely identifying something as good. The word appears once in the Greek LXX corpus, in Wisdom 7:22, so its precise force there depends on the surrounding verse and passage.
